description: Controlled forced-choice stimuli for optional live LLM analogy selection. Each family includes near, far, surface-trap, and unrelated candidates. The critical comparison is far structural match versus surface trap.

items.source: A software platform sends so many low-value security alerts that engineers learn to ignore them. A later alert corresponds to a real intrusion, but the team dismisses it because the warning channel has lost credibility.

candidates.near: A hospital monitor produces frequent false alarms. Nurses become desensitized and react too slowly when a real emergency alarm occurs.
candidates.far: A shepherd repeatedly gives false warnings about a wolf. Villagers eventually stop trusting him, so when a real wolf appears his genuine warning is ignored.
candidates.surface_trap: A software platform upgrades its security-alert interface, making warnings larger and easier for engineers to notice; response time improves because the signal becomes more salient.
candidates.unrelated: A restaurant changes its reservation layout to seat larger groups more efficiently.

items.source: A company deliberately accepts a loss in one small market so scarce sales resources can be reassigned to two markets where the matchup is much more favorable, increasing total portfolio return.

candidates.near: A fund sells one locally profitable position to free capital for a combination of positions with better expected portfolio-level return.
candidates.far: A competitor with weaker and stronger horses deliberately sacrifices one race and changes the pairings in the others, improving the result of the whole series.
candidates.surface_trap: A company accepts losses in a small market because managers failed to notice that the product was unprofitable; the loss has no compensating effect elsewhere.
candidates.unrelated: A city repaints lane markings to make a road easier to navigate.

items.source: A bank continues using a risk model calibrated to a stable housing market after the market regime changes. The equations still run correctly, but their assumptions no longer fit the environment.

candidates.near: A forecasting system trained on one economic regime fails after policy changes alter the relationships its model assumed were stable.
candidates.far: A commander fluent in abstract military theory applies textbook assumptions without adapting to battlefield feedback, and the plan fails when real conditions violate those assumptions.
candidates.surface_trap: A bank updates a risk model after discovering a software bug in one formula; once the formula is fixed, the same market assumptions remain valid.
candidates.unrelated: A museum moves a painting to a room with better lighting.

items.source: A subscription service maximizes immediate fees so aggressively that customers leave, destroying the recurring revenue stream it was trying to monetize.

candidates.near: A game publisher extracts so much short-term spending from players that the community collapses and future revenue disappears.
candidates.far: An owner kills the goose producing golden eggs in an attempt to obtain all future value immediately, eliminating the productive asset itself.
candidates.surface_trap: A subscription service raises fees after adding features, and customers stay because they value the improved product more than the price increase.
candidates.unrelated: A school changes the font on its course catalog.

items.source: Independent teams each consume extra capacity from a shared computing service because each team receives its own benefit while congestion costs are spread across everyone; collectively the service becomes unusable.

candidates.near: Drivers individually choose the route that looks fastest, but their combined choices increase congestion and make travel worse for everyone.
candidates.far: Herders each gain by adding another animal to a shared pasture while depletion costs are distributed across the group; aggregate extraction destroys the commons.
candidates.surface_trap: Independent software teams coordinate to share one testing cluster, reducing duplicate infrastructure and improving utilization for everyone.
candidates.unrelated: A chess player studies an opponent's opening repertoire.

items.source: A political organization remains optimized for an old media environment even after public communication shifts to a new platform; routines that once created strength now slow adaptation.

candidates.near: A newspaper remains organized around print distribution after readers move online, and its legacy assets make rapid reorganization costly.
candidates.far: A photography incumbent remains tied to a profitable film-based business model while industry value shifts to digital imaging, turning legacy strengths into constraints.
candidates.surface_trap: A political organization keeps the same media strategy because the old channel remains dominant and continues producing the best results.
candidates.unrelated: A hospital replaces broken chairs in its waiting room.

items.source: A cyber defender does not fight thousands of attacking devices one by one. It disables the command infrastructure they depend on, causing the distributed attack to lose coordination.

candidates.near: A security team blocks the central credential service that a bot network needs instead of responding separately to every malicious request.
candidates.far: A relief army avoids the enemy's strongest siege line and threatens the attacker's vulnerable home base, forcing redeployment and relieving the original target indirectly.
candidates.surface_trap: A cyber attacker hides malicious code inside a trusted file so defenders voluntarily carry the threat through their own security boundary.
candidates.unrelated: A retailer changes the order of products on a shelf.

items.source: A university judges research quality mainly by paper count. Researchers respond by slicing work into many minimally distinct papers, increasing the measured output while weakening its connection to actual research quality.

candidates.near: A call center rewards agents almost entirely for calls handled per hour, so agents rush customers off the phone and the metric improves while service quality worsens.
candidates.far: A bank imposes aggressive numerical cross-selling targets, and employees create unwanted accounts to satisfy the target even though genuine customer value and trust decline.
candidates.surface_trap: A military theorist knows many written treatises about warfare but fails because abstract assumptions do not fit real battlefield conditions.
candidates.unrelated: A farmer plants flowers along a fence.

no_match_controls.source: A student chooses a blue notebook because it is on sale.
candidates: A city replaces old water pipes after routine inspection.
A chess player studies an opening before a tournament.
A museum rotates an exhibit to another room.

no_match_controls.source: A cafe changes the music volume in the afternoon.
candidates: A telescope receives a software update.
A family moves dinner thirty minutes earlier.
